source: Compton Scattering
A photon carries momentum p = h/λ, so an X-ray that bounces off an electron comes away with a longer wavelength.
Students think the scattered photon slows down, when it still moves at c and its lost energy shows up as a longer wavelength.

A photon has no mass, but it carries momentum. Turn the de Broglie relation around: a photon of wavelength $\lambda$ has $p = h/\lambda$. In 1923 Arthur Compton bounced X-rays off electrons and found that the photons behave like billiard balls in a collision, conserving both energy and momentum.

A photon has momentum $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{E}{c}$. A photon that scatters off a free electron at angle $\theta$ comes away with a longer wavelength: $$\Delta\lambda = \lambda' - \lambda = \frac{h}{m_e c}(1 - \cos\theta),$$ where $\dfrac{h}{m_e c} = 2.43\ \text{pm}$ (the Compton wavelength of the electron).
An X-ray photon strikes an electron at rest. The electron recoils, and the photon leaves with less energy and a longer wavelength.

The electron recoils and carries off some kinetic energy. The photon must lose that much energy, and for a photon less energy means a lower frequency and a longer wavelength, since $E = hc/\lambda$. Its speed cannot change: every photon moves at $c$. A head-on bounce ($\theta = 180^\circ$) gives the electron the biggest kick, so the shift is largest there, $2(2.43) = 4.86\ \text{pm}$. A grazing scatter ($\theta \to 0$) changes almost nothing.

Thinking the scattered photon slows down. It still moves at $c$; its lost energy shows up as a longer wavelength (lower frequency). Check: the shift depends only on the angle, and $\lambda'$ is always longer than $\lambda$.
X-rays of $71.0\ \text{pm}$ scatter at $90^\circ$ from free electrons. Find the scattered wavelength.
Scattering at 90°
$\cos 90^\circ = 0$, so $\Delta\lambda = 2.43\ \text{pm}$.
For the same scattering, how much kinetic energy does the electron get? Use $hc = 1240\ \text{eV·nm} = 1.240 \times 10^{6}\ \text{eV·pm}$.
Energy given to the electron
About $580\ \text{eV}$
The electron gets the difference: about $580\ \text{eV}$, so the photon gave up about $3\%$ of its energy.
